Arubo Archaeological Site is a Paleolithic open-air archaeological site located in Barangay Rio Chico, General Tinio, Nueva Ecija, Philippines. The site is recognized as one of the most significant lithic localities in Central Luzon and has contributed to the study of early human technological behavior in Island Southeast Asia.
Location and geological setting
The site is situated in the private lot of Severa and Nicanor B. Aves in Barangay Rio Chico, near the Peñaranda River within a gently undulating fluvial landscape at the foothills of the Sierra Madre. The area is characterized by the presence of abundant chert outcrops, a fine-grained siliceous rock widely used in prehistoric stone tool production.
These geological conditions suggest that Arubo functioned as both a raw material source and a tool production site, with prehistoric populations exploiting locally available stone resources.
Discovery and research
The Arubo site was first reported in 1995 by Jon Aves, who brought lithic materials to the attention of the National Museum of the Philippines. An initial inspection was conducted in 1996 by archaeologists including Eusebio Z. Dizon.
Systematic archaeological investigations were carried out from April to May 2001 as a joint project between the National Museum and the University of the Philippines Archaeological Studies Program (UP-ASP). The project included surface surveys, mapping, and controlled test excavations, and also served as a field training program for graduate students.
Excavations and findings
The 2001 investigations documented multiple loci across the site and recovered approximately 200 finds, including cores, flakes, and modified tools made primarily from locally sourced chert.
Some artefacts exhibit prepared-core and controlled flaking techniques comparable to the Levallois technique, indicating a degree of planning in stone tool production. The presence of chert outcrops and lithic debris suggests that Arubo functioned as a workshop or production area.
One of the most significant discoveries is a proto-handaxe, a bifacially worked large cutting tool resembling early Acheulean technology. The Acheulean tradition is generally dated from approximately 1.76 million to around 200,000 years ago during the Lower Paleolithic period.
Interpretation
Arubo is interpreted as a lithic production and activity site used by prehistoric hunter-gatherers. The spatial clustering of artefacts near raw material sources supports repeated or sustained use of the locality.
Although the site remains undated, studies by Alfred F. Pawlik and Eusebio Z. Dizon have suggested that the assemblage may belong to the Early to Middle Pleistocene, based on technological characteristics and comparisons with regional lithic industries.
Significance
The Arubo site is significant in Southeast Asian archaeology due to the presence of bifacially worked tools, including the proto-handaxe. These findings are important in discussions of the Movius Line, a hypothesis proposed by Hallam L. Movius that suggested the absence of Acheulean handaxe traditions east of India.
Discoveries at Arubo, together with comparable assemblages such as those from the Bose Basin in China, have contributed to the reassessment of early human technological diversity in Asia.
Subsequent syntheses by Pawlik have placed Arubo within broader discussions of prehistoric hunter-gatherer adaptations in the Philippines, highlighting the variability of lithic traditions in the region.
Academic and institutional impact
The 2001 Arubo field school coincided with the establishment of the Lithic Studies Laboratory at the University of the Philippines Diliman, informally opened in September 2001 and formally inaugurated in February 2002. Materials and data from Arubo were among the earliest assemblages analyzed in the facility, contributing to the development of lithic studies in the Philippines.
